title: JavaScript events versus C# delegates and events
hook: C# events are typed multicast delegates with access control on raise. JavaScript uses string-named listeners on EventEmitter or DOM EventTarget — flexible, untyped unless you wrap them.

blocks.text: A C# **delegate** is a typed function pointer; an **event** restricts who can invoke (only the declaring class raises). **Multicast** combines handlers with +=. JavaScript **EventEmitter.on/emit** allows any code with the emitter reference to emit. DOM **addEventListener** uses event objects with bubbling. JS favors **duck-typed callbacks**; C# favors **compile-time delegate signatures** and **EventHandler<TEventArgs>** patterns.

entries.plainDefinition: Type-safe reference to a method with matching signature.
Delegate holding multiple methods — all invoked on call.
Built-in delegate types — Action returns void, Func returns TResult.
entries.example: Func<int, int, int> add = (a, b) => a + b;

blocks.text: Full-stack engineers map **Blazor @onclick** to DOM listeners and **IHostedService** cancellation to AbortSignal. Misunderstanding causes double subscriptions in C# (`+=` without `-=`) or runaway JS listeners. Interviews test whether you know **who can emit**, **sync vs async handlers**, and **exception propagation** — unhandled exception in one multicast delegate aborts rest in C#; JS emitter continues unless you wrap.

blocks.title: Interview trap: event vs delegate field
blocks.body: Public delegate field allows external Invoke — event keyword prevents outside raise. JS emit is always public on the object — encapsulation is convention only.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Subscribe
items.body: C# handler += OnPaid; JS emitter.on('paid', onPaid).

items.title: Unsubscribe
items.body: C# handler -= OnPaid; JS emitter.off('paid', onPaid).

items.title: Raise
items.body: C# OnPaid?.Invoke(this, args); JS emitter.emit('paid', payload).

items.title: Typing
items.body: C# compile-time; JS runtime + optional TS wrapper.

diagram.title: C# event vs JS emitter
diagram.source:
flowchart TD

  subgraph JS[JS EventEmitter]
    S2[on event handler] --> R2[Any holder can emit]

  end

snippet.label: C# event with controlled raise
snippet.explanation: event keyword restricts Invoke to declaring type — JS has no equivalent enforcement.

snippet.label: DOM addEventListener parallel
snippet.explanation: Same subscribe/unsubscribe model as +=/-= but with capture options and event object.

snippet.label: Failure mode: delegate leak in C#
snippet.explanation: Same leak pattern as JS on() without off — GC keeps subscriber alive via delegate chain.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming JS events are typed like C#. Using async void event handlers in C# without try/catch. Forgetting -= / off and leaking subscribers. External emit on JS bus breaking invariants.

blocks.text: Architecture: domain events in C# often use MediatR or message bus with records; JS microservices use RabbitMQ/SQS — in-process EventEmitter is not cross-service. WeakEventManager in WPF solves delegate leaks; JS uses AbortSignal, WeakRef, or framework cleanup (useEffect return). Know **Func<Task>** for async C# event handlers properly.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying they are identical. Not knowing C# event vs public delegate field. Cannot explain multicast leak in both ecosystems.

interviewTakeaways: C# event: typed multicast, only owner raises. JS emit: public, string events.
Handler exceptions: C# may abort multicast chain; JS continues unless wrapped.
60s: Delegates are typed function refs. Events restrict Invoke. JS EventEmitter/DOM is duck-typed pub/sub. Both leak if you never unsubscribe.
Follow-up: design typed order events in TS mimicking C# EventHandler.
commonPitfalls: Treating JS string events as compile-time safe without TS wrapper.
Public delegate field in C# allowing external Invoke — confuse with event.
Strong answer: access control on raise, multicast, leak via retained handlers, DOM third model.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS generics on event map approximate C# EventHandler<T> — still erases at runtime.
JS callbacks/delegates are just functions passed around — no delegate keyword required.
